div.head: Chapter 8
div.p: § 8 Fourth Principle — follows from the preceding ones.

The Holy Apostolic See, in granting the said principality and imperial superiority over that Indian world to our Catholic kings of Castile and León, did not intend to deprive the natural kings and lords of that said new world of their royal states and dominions and jurisdictions, honors, and dignities, nor to grant our Catholic kings any license or faculty by which they might do, or fail to do, anything by which the spreading of the faith would be frustrated, and any obstacle placed before the Gospel, such that the conversion and salvation of those peoples would be entirely impeded or delayed, which is what Christ and his vicar intend as their principal end.

This fourth principle is proved by many reasons and means. The first is through the proof of the fourth category of unbelievers (§§ 4, 5, and 6), where it was established that those peoples stand outside all temporal and spiritual jurisdiction of the Church and of every member of it. Because we have nothing to do with them for good or ill, beyond loving them and being diligent in bringing them to the knowledge of God.

The second, it is proved by the preceding principle and its demonstration, where it was shown that the sole and final cause of the said concession was the preaching of the faith and the conversion of those peoples. For this is not a sufficient, examined, and necessary cause to deprive unbelievers of their goods, kingdoms, honors, dignities, states, and dominions. Because without depriving unbelievers of their states, honors, goods, and dominions the faith can be preached and the conversion of peoples achieved. Indeed, as is manifest, depriving them of their dominions and goods would be a most efficacious cause for disturbing the whole world and giving them reason to regard the law of Christ and the Christian religion as most unjust, and to bear it the gravest hatred, and to regard the King of heaven who founded it as a tyrant and the greatest enemy of the human race. And out of the justified fear of losing their goods, dignities, and honors, they would have the most rightful claim to make war upon us and destroy us. Therefore it must not be presumed that the Apostolic See intended to deprive the natural kings and lords of that world, through the concession it made to the kings of León and Castile, of anything, nor to give them faculty to do, or to fail to do, anything that would disturb the unbelievers and turn them against the faith, and give them occasion to blaspheme Jesus Christ himself.

The third, by the same foundation: the sole and final cause of the said concession was the promulgation of the Gospel and the preaching of the faith and the conversion of those peoples. Now, to achieve any end, the means proportionate to it must of necessity be chosen and adopted, and everything that can impede it must be avoided, according to the Philosopher, book 2 of the Physics; and to leave them in their states and preserve those states for them, and even to increase them, and to give them the faith freely, as Christ ordained, and other possible goods: this was and is a means proportionate for the Gospel to be preached without obstacle and for unbelievers to receive the faith willingly; and to deprive them of those things would be to impede forever, to frustrate and totally destroy the said end. Therefore it must not be presumed that the Apostolic See intended, through the said concession of superiority over that world to the kings of Castile, to deprive the natural kings and lords of their goods, states, and dominions.

The fourth, because the Apostolic See, through its laws or constitutions, privileges and donations, is not and never was accustomed to remove, revoke, or suspend without legitimate and necessary cause the rights, honors, and things belonging to men by natural law, by the law of nations, and by divine law; rather it professes to preserve and inviolably defend them, even though it should shed blood and lose life in doing so, as appears from the chapter sunt quidam, 25, q. 1. And if the Apostolic See is not accustomed without legitimate cause to deprive anyone of their property however small, much less of their honors and dignities and of what belongs to their persons: argument, ff, De poenis, L. in servorum; as argued by Andreas of Isernia, in the title Que sint regalia, L. vectigalia, 3. col. For if it intended to deprive the kings and lords of that world of their states and dominions through the said concession or donation, it would be depriving them without legitimate cause of their rights and honors and dignities belonging to them by natural law, by the law of nations, and by divine law, as has been said, which ought not to be thought of the Holy See, and still less said. Therefore, through the said donation, the Holy See did not intend to deprive them of their goods, honors, and dominions, etc.

Let the fifth reason be what Dominicus of San Gimignano says in his eleventh consilium, and he says thus: that whenever the pope grants some new right, it is not to be understood that his intention is to take away the right that some third party previously held. Because it is always to be understood, and must be understood, that if the pope grants anything, it is without prejudice to another's right, ut in c. super eo, De officio delegati, et De rescriptis, c. quamvis et c. si propter tua debita, Lib. 6; and what is more, he says, even if he adds words referring to a past fault, saying that a preceding fault may be opposed, through these general words it is not the pope's intention to take away the right of another — which is very much to be noted — unless he says so specifically: said c. quamvis; et De consuetudine, c. cum olim. All of this is from Dominicus, and to it may be added the reasoning of those texts: that injuries should not arise from where rights arise: l. meminerint, Codex, De vi et vi armata. In granting, therefore, to the kings of Castile and León the universal empire and superiority over that Indian world, the vicar of Christ did not intend to deprive the kings and lords of those peoples — whose world that is and not ours — of their kingdoms, states, dignities, and dominions, nor any private person of their goods; nor did the pope give them faculty to do or to allow anything by which the preaching of the faith would be frustrated and some obstacle placed before the Gospel and the conversion of souls impeded; but rather that, as universal princes and lords in favor of the faith, the natural kings should remain with their immediate governments and dominions. For the one lordship and the other are very well compatible, as we proved in our Tractado Comprobatorio in the same fashion, which we dedicated to King Philip, our king and lord, while he was still prince. And thus the fourth principle appears to be proved.
